body: Loughran & McDonald (J. Finance 2011): about 3/4 of Harvard-IV 'negative' words (tax, cost, liability) are not negative in 10-Ks. Their finance-specific list of 2,337 negative words relates to filing returns, volatility, fraud and material weakness, so generic sentiment tools should not be used on filings. Their readability paper shows the Fog index is poorly specified for finance; file size is a better proxy. Li (JAE 45, 2008): lower-earnings firms write longer, harder-to-read annual reports, and readable reports go with more persistent profits. Price, Doran, Peterson & Bliss (JBF 2012): US call tone predicts abnormal returns and volume and outweighs the earnings surprise over 60 days. Bushee, Gow & Taylor (JAR 2018; 60,172 calls): complexity mixes obfuscation and real information, and analysts' question complexity can benchmark it. Larcker & Zakolyukina (JAR 2012): deceptive executives use more general-knowledge phrases, fewer shareholder-value references, and CEOs use more extreme positive words; models beat random by 6-16%, and the most-deceptive-CFO portfolio had -4% to -11% annual alpha. Mayew & Venkatachalam (JF 2012): negative vocal affect predicts misses over 3 quarters, but the LVA software is disputed. Use these as within-company trend features and red flags, not as standalone signals.
title: Text and tone research: LM dictionary, readability, call tone, obfuscation, deception
